Weekly News Summary.
The railroads have reduced the fare from New York to Chicago to $11. The scalpers are selling at $9.

The recent daily mortality at St. Louis from the heat and other causes has approximated epidemic figures.

A BALD-EAGLE was recently caught at Wilmington, Delaware, while trying to carry off a large Newfoundland dog.

The Japanese mikado is to have a new palace at Yeddo, which is to be entirely of wood, and will cost nearly $5,600,000.

LOUISVILLE, July 27.—A special to the Commercial from Tiptonville, Tenn., says Felix Wyley, colored, was taken from jail by one hundred and fifty masked men and lynched. TIPTONVILLE, TENN., July 28.—One Felix Wyley, a large, black, desperate negro, was taken out of jail at this place between 8 and 9 o'clock Monday night and hanged. He had been in this community a year or more, and came here from Union City, where he killed a man and put him on the railroad. He was also an escaped convict from Nashville, prior to coming to Union City. He boasted to some of his most intimate acquaintances of these facts, and that he had committed a rape on a woman, and would not stand back to kill anybody, black or white. He committed a rape upon the body of a young white lady and then murdered her, on the evening of July 13th. The young lady had been to town and was returning home when seized upon by the black fiend, and after accomplishing his aim destroyed her life to hide his deed. After the young lady was discovered missing search was made for her, but with no success, until more than a week afterward, when a portion of her body was found near the road. The hogs and dogs had devoured it, leaving only a part of the bones, her fan, parasol, and hat to mark the spot where the hellish act was perpetrated. This negro gave good reasons for suspicion, and after finding her remains he was arrested and placed in jail. A number of men appeared at the jail Sunday night and demanded Sheriff Pittman to surrender his prisoner, and it was only through the most earnest appeals by the Sheriff that saved the prisoner's life then. Mr. Pittman asked them to wait until next day and let the negro have his preliminary trial before taking his life. They finally concluded to do so, but assuring him that they intended to have the prisoner to-morrow (Monday) night if they had to burn the jail. The negro had his trial the following day, and the chain of circumstantial evidence was so strong and conclusive against him that they more firmly resolved to put him to death that night. A large number of people were in town during the trial, and much interest was made manifest over the occasion. Everything being made ready, a band of about fifty men, white and black, suddenly made their appearance before the Sheriff and Jailer, and ordered of him the keys. He had summoned a number of our citizens as guards that night, but only a few of them had arrived before the mob dashed in, and that is why the mob was successful in reaching the jail and surrounding the sheriff and his posses. The Nashville American of yesterday has the following special telegram from Hickman: "Reliable information from Tiptonville, Tennessee, thirty miles below here on the Mississippi river, gives the particulars of a horrible crime and its punishment by mob law. A few days ago the body of an orphan girl, — Hall, who had been missing for ten days, was found in a fence corner near the public road, bearing evidences that she had been ravished and murdered in the most shocking manner. juan-morales-phoenix-1881-08-14.A5: A shooting affray took place in the upper town of Tempe yesterday, resulting in the death of Juan Nagrels at the hands of Santos Morales—both parties being Mexicans. The particulars of the affair, as gleaned by a Gazette reporter from an interview with Manuel Gallardo, the officer who made the arrest, are as follows: Some six weeks ago Nagrels, who it is said was formerly a Lieutenant of Marquez Mexican handits, came to Tempe and shortly thereafter made the acquaintance of Morales and family. His attentions to Mrs. Morales soon became so marked as to arouse the distrust and jealousy of her husband, who forbade Nagrels visiting the house. But remonstrances and threats proved alike of no avail—Nagrels appeared more amused than otherwise, and persisted in his visits. Morales complained to Constable Gallardo of the matter, but no steps could be taken to prevent these intrusions as Tempe was without a Justice of the Peace at the time. On Sunday morning Morales returned home to find his wife and Nagrels in social converse, and his rage knew no bounds. He informed the destroyer of his domestic peace and happiness that he would take the law in his own hands. The latter only laughed, while the self-supposed outraged husband went about to prepare for his bloody work. Liberal potations of forty-rod whisky served to produce the necessary courage, and a six-shooter furnished the instrument of death. At four o'clock Morales was in good condition to assume the leading role in most any tragedy, and it was at this hour that he met Nagrels, in Gallardo's saloon. Morales addressed Nagrels with the remark, "Now I am going to kill you." It is evident that the latter recognized that the remark was made in earnest, for he started to run just as Morales drew his revolver. The first shot missed Nagrels, but the second ball struck him just above the left shoulder blade, coming out on the opposite side above the collar bone. In two minutes he lay dead upon the floor—another victim to jealousy and strong drink. —Gazette.

THE REFRIGERATING APPARATUS A SUCCESS.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The success achieved by the refrigerating apparatus insures the uniform temperature of the sick room and adds another feature to the favorable circumstances surrounding the case. By means of a steam fan, air is blown over tons of ice, and the air comes immediately into the room, and it is possible to reduce the temperature to fifty-four degrees. This morning it is at seventy-five degrees, and the doctors have ordered the engine to run slower, as the room is cool enough. None of the other appliances will be used.

VERY LITTLE DANGER FROM SECONDARY HEMORRHAGE.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The doctors are free to say to-day that the danger from secondary hemorrhage, if not quite past, is now very slight. Indeed, only some unforeseen accident is likely to precipitate that trouble. The doctors have the very best anti-septic dressing at hand and the most improved instruments of all kinds for any emergency. They do not expect pyemia as a direct result of the wound since the channel made by the ball is so isolated by nature as to forefend that complication. The pus corpuscles are too large for absorption into the virus, hence only an accident will produce trouble from that quarter. Thus it will be seen that the immediate danger of the presidents condition is virtually past. The healing process is progressing as far as the preliminary inflammation is concerned and all the patient needs is to have his system kept up to an improving standard, and have close watch kept on every symptom and be made as comfortable as possible. His nourishment is continued in gradually increased quantities. One or more of the physicians is constantly near him and no efforts have been spared to add to his comfort. This thorough system will be continued indefinitely and its effect in the opinion of the doctors will be the patients final recovery.

MORE "CRANKS" IN WASHINGTON.

WASHINGTON, July 11.—The name "cranks" is having a national ventilation lately. They are showing up at the capital promiscuously. The latest arrival is Matilda Bascomb (colored), who was arrested on the square fronting the White House this morning. She had been hanging around the White House grounds for some time, acting strangely and talking wildly. She was taken to the police headquarters, where she declared herself as a warm personal friend of ex-President Hayes. The latter, she maintained, was still president. Her business with him was to collect the interest every week on money loaned Mr. Hayes by her shortly after he entered upon his administration, Gen. Garfield's wound, she claims, was by no means as represented. It was only a flesh wound, but the physicians had exaggerated the case to make political capital. She was sent to the insane asylum.

Another of the same kind, Hannah D. Klunger, came to the police headquarters and inquired for directions as to how she could find the attorney-general. The woman, when questioned, said that she had been swindled by lawyers out of all her property in Bay City, Mich., and that she had name here to see the attorney-general to compel him to have it restored. She said she knew he would do it because President Garfield had refused to do what was right and had been punished and that the same would befall officials who would not listen to the cry of a distressed people. A letter to President Garfield was found amongst her baggage, which contained the clause: "I kindly ask you to send some Christian preachers to look after the wicked town of Bay City, Michigan, and reform its sinful citizens. The rest of the story was composed of attacks on Attorney-General McVeagh and President Garfield, and threats against them, mixed with mourning over the sinful lawyers of Bay City.

The physicians in the president's case seem to leave most of the talking to Dr. Bliss, but they agree with him in its general aspect and almost every particular. His latest remarks on the special features of the case have been in regard to the location of the ball.

He says there are now certain indications which make it probable that they can remove the ball without danger. "At present," says the doctor, "we deem it prudent to withhold them, but they are such as to make it clear that the track of the ball was rightly stated in the first diagnosis. We know where the ball entered the body. We have felt and developed the course of the ball so far. Where it went we do not definitely know, but from the direction of three inches of the course, which has been ascertained, it is certain that it must have flied the liver and probably passed entirely through the abdominal cavity and it is lodged in the interior wall of the abdomen. That is where I think it now, in the interior wall of the abdomen and not in the abdominal cavity. The ball entering the body where it did, and passing inward three inches, must of necessity pass through a portion of the liver. At that point of the body the liver lies close alongside of the ribs and a ball could not penetrate the body at that point and enter so great a distance and strike the liver. The liver is there and must have been hit. Even if the ball dropped downward afterward it must have grazed the liver in its downward course, but, as I said, the indications of which we have privately advised Drs. Agnew and Hamilton by letter, are that the ball went through the liver to the abdominal cavity and is lodged in the interior wall of the abdomen, as at first supposed, and it will be easy, when the time comes, to remove it from that point without danger.

MULISH JURORS.
Complications Growing Out of the Edisto Trouble.
the correspondent of the Savannah News, who has just returned from the scene of the reported troubles on Edisto Island, reports that quiet has been restored, although the body of the dead man has not yet been interred, and a perfect understanding and peace will not take place until an inquest is held. The negroes believe that the dead man died from the effects of injuries received by him in a scuffle with a white boy, which is not probable, and asked that an autopsy be made. The physician was ready to make the autopsy, but could not do it without the order of the Deputy Coroner, who refused to order it. The negroes on the jury thereupon refused to agree to a verdict or to bury the body, which still lies in the open air.

A great many of the whites attribute the blame of the excitement to the Deputy Coroner, who does not seem to know his business. The whole matter could be settled by the sending down of a Deputy Coroner to hold an inquest after an autopsy, and it is hoped that this will be done. When the correspondent left the island this noon the negroes were at work as usual, and there were no signs of a disturbance, although an uneasy feeling prevails.

The cause of the trouble, as told by the constable, is that on the 1st instant Mr. Marlon Seabrook and his brother, Mr. Harry Seabrook, sons of Mr. Edward W. Seabrook, got into a difficulty with the negro Wilson Calder, who used such language towards them that Mr. Marlon Seabrook struck him with his fist. A regular fisticuff ensued in which it appears that Mr. Harry Seabrook picked up a brick, but did not use it. The next day Calder went about his work as usual and ploughed in the field all day with out complaining of any ill effects from the fight. On the night of the 2d instant, when he went home, he is said to have eaten a potful of parboiled hominy, and the next morning he died.

Mr. Seabrook Whaley organized a Coroner's jury, consisting of seven white men and five negroes and started to hold the inquest. The negroes, became very much excited and claimed that the man had been killed by Mr. Seabrook during the fight on the 1st instant. Ten witnesses were examined, including Dr. Murray, who held an external examination of the body, and who testified that there were no marks of violence on the body, except a bad burn between the shoulders, which it was proved the deceased had recently received by falling into the fire during an epileptic fit, to which disease he was subject.

The negroes, however, were not satisfied with the doctor's testimony, and insisted that the jury should bring in a verdict of willful murder. This, of course, the jury refused to do, and the negroes then refused to allow the body to be buried until it was opened and an examination made to discover if there were any internal injuries. Dr. Murray, it appears, was not well and insisted that the opening of the body was entirely useless. The negroes then became more violent, and the jury dispersed without arriving at a result.

The crops on the island are better than they have ever been known to be before at this time of the year.
